St. Barlaam of Serpukhov

Saint Barlaam of Serpukhov

St. Barlaam of Serpukhov · St. Varlaam of Serpukhov · St. Varlaam Serpukhovsky

Period
Fourteenth century; traditional repose 1377
Region
Moscow; Serpukhov, Russia
Titles / vocation
Monastic · Abbot
Commemoration
May 5

Introduction

Saint Barlaam was a monk connected with Saint Alexis of Moscow and the establishment of the Vladychny Monastery at Serpukhov.

Read the published life [1]

BackgroundLife and notable eventsDeath and martyrdomWritings and legacyChronology
Death / martyrdom

Peaceful repose traditionally dated May 5, 1377

Read circumstances and sources

Background

The Russian Church’s monastic department says that his birthplace, parents, and place of tonsure are unknown. Its narrative begins in 1360. He served as the cell attendant of Saint Alexis, the metropolitan.

[1] Official ecclesiastical biography / teaching / commemoration · Opening paragraphs on lost origins and relationship with Alexis

Life and notable events

The monastery’s tradition attributes its establishment to a command heard from an icon of the Theotokos. Saint Alexis sent Saint Barlaam to find a site. Saint Barlaam oversaw construction and the emerging monastic community; the account includes visions and miraculous events.

[1] Official ecclesiastical biography / teaching / commemoration · Foundation narrative and paragraphs on building the monastery

Death and martyrdom

The received life describes blindness and failing health near the end of his life. It dates his peaceful repose to May 5, 1377, and says Saint Alexis buried him at the church porch. It does not describe martyrdom.

[1] Official ecclesiastical biography / teaching / commemoration · Paragraphs on blindness, final illness and burial

Writings and legacy

His memory is preserved chiefly through the monastery’s founding narrative and veneration. Much of his earlier biography was not recorded. The OCA calendar independently commemorates him on May 5.

[1] Official ecclesiastical biography / teaching / commemoration · Introductory account of the monastery chronicle and later memorial tradition
